narrative:
The model estimated a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that risk estimate crossed the threshold used for admission, your application was rejected. This is a probability-based risk assessment, not a certainty that you will fail.

The strongest factor behind the decision was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile, so this sharply pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 39. Although it was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37, it pushed toward passing and worked in your favor—but it was not enough to outweigh the academic-standing concern. The third most influential factor was your first-year class standing: again the lowest decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, which also pushed toward failure.

To move forward, ask admissions whether you may discuss the decision or any appeal process. Strengthen your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a graduate program, and prepare to retake the LSAT if feasible. Seek pre-law advising to build a clear improvement plan, then reapply with evidence of stronger preparation and context for your early class ranks.
